newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's prime minister -- sacked or sick?.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's prime minister -- sacked or sick?.

text.p: Prime ministers have come and gone on an annual basis in post-Soviet Ukraine, but the scenario which apparently saw off Pavlo Lazarenko entered the realms of the bizarre on Friday.
Neither the government's nor the president's offices could say what was wrong with the prime minister, who was delivered to a government hospital on Thursday and simultaneously removed from his post.
His deputy Vasyl Durdynets was appointed acting prime minister by presidential decree "for the time of his illness", but there were varying accounts of what that illness was.

A senior doctor at the hospital said Lazarenko was suffering from an extreme form of varicose veins which can lead to a stroke. But his top aide, Ihor Hrytsyak, told UNIAN news agency he was suffering from "physical and psychological exhaustion".
Other aides said Lazarenko, 44, had been well on Thursday and that the illness issue was just a ploy to get rid of him.
"I unfortunately have no idea what kind of illness he has," presidential spokesman Dmytro Markov told reporters.

Lazarenko is Ukraine's fifth prime minister since it won independence from Moscow in 1991, or sixth if a long-term acting premier is counted. In May 1996 he replaced Yevhen Marchuk, who was accused of mishandling the economy and self-promotion.

Diplomatic and business sources say President Leonid Kuchma has come under mounting pressure from Western officials and investors to sack Lazarenko, blamed in part for slow privatisation and failing to stamp out government corruption.

Kuchma has criticised the goverment recently for failing to push through reforms and this year's budget, measures Ukraine needs to qualify for a multi-billion-dollar payment from the International Monetary Fund.

The Fund's deputy managing director, Stanley Fischer, met Kuchma on Thursday and Friday and was quoted by the president's top economic aide as saying the loan could be approved in July if deputies passed the budget in time.
Meanwhile the fate of Lazarenko -- an imposing, dark-haired, bespectacled figure -- was shrouded in mystery.
Volodymyr Svyrydov, chief doctor at the elite Feofaniya hospital outside Kiev, said Lazarenko had been brought there but he was "not in a serious condition".
"He has varicose veins in the legs and aggravated chronic thrombo-phlebitis," the doctor said by telephone.
Thrombo-phlebitis -- swollen veins with clot formation -- can lead to a stroke or even a heart attack if it is untreated.
"It is very likely that Lazarenko will have an operation to remove the veins," Sviridov said.

Whatever was wrong with Lazarenko -- who has been repeatedly accused in the press of having a stake in the lucrative energy sector, a charge he denies -- local media were clearly tired on Friday of months of reporting on his impending dismissal.
They started speculating on who could replace him.
The respected Den daily newspaper noted that constitutionally, Kuchma could appoint an acting prime minister for 60 days but after that he would need a majority approval in parliament.
So First Deputy Prime Minister Vasyl Durdynets could stay in charge until the budget is passed and parliament closes its doors in mid-July until it reconvenes in early September.
But Den added that Kuchma could later reinstate Lazarenko.
Analysts say potential replacements could include Anatoly Kinakh, head of the Ukrainian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs led by Kuchma when he ran for president in 1994.
Durdynets, a former police general considered to be politically weak, is not seen as a likely long-term replacement as he is unpopular in parliament.
Den favoured Serhiy Tyhypko, Deputy Prime Minister in charge of reforms, as a better candidate "who has the image of a young reformer who has not been sullied by a long spell in power".
Tyhypko was appointed in April after Viktor Pynzenyk resigned in disgust at parliament's failure to pass reforms.
